text:
Wind tower gravity energy storage

The WTGES system is a hybrid infrastructure solution that integrates a gravity storage module directly within the tower of a wind turbine, functioning simultaneously as an energy storage device and an active TMD. As illustrated in Fig. 1a, the macro system consists of an auxiliary motor/generator unit housed in the nacelle, mechanically coupled to a heavy suspended mass via high-strength cables. This configuration facilitates bi-directional energy flow: lifting the mass (charging) absorbs excess grid power, while lowering it (discharging) releases gravitational potential energy to provide instantaneous inertial support.

To ensure structural integrity and operational safety, the design incorporates a realistic mechanical integration mechanism (Fig. 1b). Unlike theoretical free-hanging concepts, the suspended mass is strictly constrained by vertical guide rails to prevent uncontrolled collision with the tower shell. Crucially, the mass block is coupled with hydraulic pendulum dampers, enabling it to act as a TMD that actively dissipates wind-induced tower vibrations during operation. A bottom unloading platform equipped with safety locks is included to secure the mass during extreme weather events, unloading the cables and reverting the tower to its baseline survival mode. For a representative 10 MW offshore turbine, the system accommodates a 50-ton high-density mass (steel/iron), yielding a storage capacity of roughly 12.3 kWh. While the energy capacity is modest—comparable to a standard residential battery system—the system is strictly optimized for high-power ancillary services rather than bulk energy arbitrage (see “Methods”). This co-location strategy leverages existing tower infrastructure to minimize civil construction costs.

Frequency stability enhancement

The systematic evaluation across power classes reveals a robust correlation between system scale and intrinsic frequency stability, where the baseline maximum frequency deviation drops by 56.7% as turbine capacity scales from 10 kW (0.0358 Hz) to 10 MW (0.0155 Hz) (Fig. 2a), reflecting the stabilizing role of higher rotor inertia. Integrating WTGES further suppresses frequency excursions, consistently reducing the maximum deviation by 11–16% and the peak-to-peak amplitude by 5–15% across all scales (Fig. 2a, d). Notably, the discharging mode outperforms the charging mode in mitigating frequency nadirs (Fig. 2c); for instance, in the 10 kW microgrid scenario, the discharging operation restricts deviation to 0.0301 Hz compared to 0.0319 Hz in charging mode (Fig. 2a). This performance edge is physically attributed to the unidirectional inertial characteristics of the rope-driven system: under the simulated declining wind speed conditions (9–6 m s−1), the descending mass (Discharging) synergizes gravitational potential energy release with motor inertia to inject active power, whereas the ascending mass (Charging) faces mechanical limitations in reversing kinematic states to counter power deficits.

While WTGES effectively clamps large-amplitude excursions, a trade-off is observed in signal smoothness, quantified by the frequency root mean square (RMS) (Fig. 2b). Unlike the BES system in the 101 MW cluster, which achieves the lowest RMS (0.0012 Hz) due to its lag-free electrochemical response, the WTGES introduces a slight elevation in RMS values relative to the baseline (e.g., rising from 0.0030 to 0.0033 Hz in the 10 MW case) (Fig. 2b). This phenomenon stems from the discrete physical constraints of the mechanical architecture: strict jerk limitations prevent instantaneous power steps, and millisecond-scale mechanical latencies in the drivetrain introduce phase lags that manifest as high-frequency harmonic distortions. Consequently, while the asymmetric regulation of WTGES successfully arrests dangerous frequency drifts, the inherent mechanical “roughness” results in a higher RMS compared to the pristine response of inverter-based electronic storage. This highlights a fundamental distinction: WTGES functions less as a precision instrument for minor fluctuations and more as a robust “inertial airbag” for arresting severe frequency excursions.

Structural integrity and active damping performance

To validate the feasibility of suspending a heavy mass within the nacelle, we integrated a high-fidelity 2-degree-of-freedom (2-DOF) dynamic model calibrated to an IEA 10 MW direct-drive reference turbine. Standard offshore towers are typically designed with substantial safety margins (often exceeding 50%) to withstand rare extreme events, leaving significant structural capacity idle during normal operation. The WTGES exploits this by employing a “margin exchange” strategy: while the suspended mass occupies a fraction of this static capacity (~10%), its function as an active TMD significantly mitigates dynamic loads. Consequently, the system “returns” more safety margin through vibration suppression than it consumes via added weight, transforming the storage mass from a static burden into a dynamic stabilizer, a synergy we define as “structural value stacking.”

Time-domain simulations under turbulent wind conditions demonstrate that this active inertial control effectively clamps tower motion, reducing the RMS displacement by 62.4% (from 0.65 to 0.24 m) and—crucially for drivetrain reliability—suppressing peak nacelle acceleration by 56.6% (from 5.17 to 2.24 m s−2) (Fig. 3a, b). This vibration mitigation translates to a significant reduction in primary dynamic fatigue loads, establishing a theoretical upper bound of a nearly 50-fold extension in the tower’s fatigue life under idealized linear damage accumulation (Supplementary Note 5). Furthermore, the control strategy exhibits exceptional engineering robustness; spectral analysis confirms that the system maintains a suppression efficiency exceeding 50% even under stiffness parameter drifts of ±10% (Fig. 3c). This creates a broad “safety island” in the frequency-damping landscape (Fig. 3d) that accommodates not only real-world manufacturing tolerances but also potential structural aging, providing a robust buffer to maintain critical safety margins from the turbine’s 1P and 3P frequency exclusion zones throughout its service life.

To balance structural benefits against static gravity loads, sensitivity analysis identifies a 100-ton suspended mass as the optimal design point, located at the “knee” of the performance curve where marginal damping gains begin to diminish (Fig. 3e). Note that while the 50-ton mass introduced earlier server as a conservative baseline for energy capacity estimation, this 100-ton configuration is specifically evaluated to maximize the active damping effect. Survivability under 50-year extreme operating gusts (EOGs) is prioritized through the Tier-3 fail-safe unloading mechanism (“Methods”). As shown in Fig. 3f, the system decouples and locks the mass to the base upon gust detection. This critical intervention prevents the amplification of P-Delta effects, keeping the maximum transient displacement (3.36 m) safely within the tower’s elastic limit with a drift ratio of only 0.76%, thereby indicating that the addition of the storage mass can be managed without compromising the structural safety of the wind turbine under survival conditions.

Techno-economic assessment and value stacking

While the structural synergy of the WTGES has been validated, its widespread adoption hinges on demonstrating commercial viability against mature competitors like lithium-ion batteries (WTBES). A critical economic skepticism regarding gravity storage is whether the incremental capital expenditure (CAPEX) of structural integration outweighs the revenue from grid services. However, traditional levelized cost of storage (LCOS) models often overlook the “hidden value” of asset longevity. By internalizing the fatigue life extension—demonstrated in Fig. 4—as a projected reduction in operational expenditure (OPEX), we propose a holistic valuation framework. This approach reframes the WTGES not merely as an energy storage device, but as a dual-function asset where the cost of mass is shared by two distinct value streams: regulation services and structural protection.

To assess the commercial feasibility of WTGES, we performed a comprehensive techno-economic analysis across turbine scales ranging from 3.4 to 20 MW (Fig. 4). Our results reveal that the incremental CAPEX for WTGES is dominated by the mass block and hoisting system, accounting for approximately ~80% of the total cost (Fig. 4a). Crucially, this cost scales linearly with turbine capacity, benefiting from the direct reuse of the existing tower infrastructure which eliminates the civil engineering expenses typical of standalone storage. The economic case is solidified by the unique “value stacking” mechanism (Fig. 4b): beyond standard revenues from frequency regulation and inertial support, WTGES projects a distinct theoretical “OPEX saving” stream potentially accounting for 60–70% of the total annual value-stacking revenue (comprising ancillary services and structural benefits)—by functioning as an active TMD that reduces structural fatigue maintenance costs.

A lifecycle net present value (NPV) comparison for a representative 15 MW system confirms this advantage (Fig. 4c). The WTGES trajectory (blue line) consistently outperforms the battery system (WTBES, gray dashed line) primarily due to its significantly lower initial CAPEX enabled by infrastructure sharing. Furthermore, while the WTBES suffers a sharp value erosion in year 10 due to mandatory cell replacement costs (red dotted line), the WTGES maintains a robust, monotonically increasing return profile, leveraging the long service life of electromechanical components. Sensitivity analysis (Fig. 4d) further indicates that the project’s NPV is most sensitive to tariff and efficiency, while variations in total CAPEX have a comparatively muted impact, demonstrating economic robustness against construction cost uncertainties.

Finally, mapping the cost structure of WTGES against established technologies (Fig. 4e) reveals a distinct economic dichotomy. While physical height constraints result in a relatively high energy storage cost (2611–5807 USD kWh−1)—approximately 15 times that of lithium-ion batteries (150–450 USD kWh−1)—the system maintains a highly competitive power cost (247–607 USD kW−1). Although this range is higher than supercapacitors, it remains significantly below Pumped Hydro (800–2500 USD kW−1) and sits in the same tier as Li-ion batteries and flywheels. This positioning is further reinforced by the LCOS gradient, where the relatively high LCOS of WTGES (~0.72 USD kWh−1) contrasts sharply with bulk storage solutions like pumped hydro (~0.04 USD kWh−1) and Li-ion batteries (~0.06 USD kWh−1). This cost structure explicitly restricts WTGES from energy arbitrage applications, dictating its optimal deployment in high-frequency power regulation where cycle life outweighs energy capacity costs. From a design perspective, WTGES targets high energy efficiency, zero self-discharge, and a theoretical mechanical cycle life exceeding 10 million cycles (subject to regular cable and damper maintenance). This unique combination of mechanical durability and competitive power costs places WTGES firmly within the “Power Services” domain (blue zone). Clustering with flywheels and Li-ion batteries, it fills a crucial gap for inertial support where electrochemical batteries (orange zone) are economically burdened by cycle degradation and replacement costs.

This study proposes and validates a Structure-Grid Synergy framework that reuses wind turbine tower infrastructure. It integrates GES with TMD to overcome limitations of traditional single-function energy storage evaluations. We validated it across scales from 300 to 101 MW. The results indicate that WTGES can effectively compensate for inertia shortfalls in high-penetration renewable energy grids. Moreover, it significantly enhances the structural resilience of ultra-large wind turbines through passive physical damping. This multifunctional integration presents a promising physical inertia solution for future deep offshore wind farms. It features low power costs and minimizes the need for additional land acquisition.

We address potential structural instability risks from suspending large masses within the tower through a Margin Exchange mechanism. The mass increases static compressive stress by approximately 10%. However, its role as a passive TMD effectively mitigates dynamic responses induced by wind loads. Simulation results show that the system reduces tower RMS displacement by 62.4% and suppresses nacelle peak acceleration by 56.6%. This vibration suppression effect directly translates into a substantial reduction in fatigue loads. Therefore, under idealized linear damage accumulation, it establishes a theoretical upper bound of nearly a 50-fold extension for the tower’s fatigue life. In addition, the system implements a safety unloading mechanism for 50-year EOGs. This provides a critical safeguard for survivability under extreme conditions. Thus, it demonstrates that the gravity storage mass can transform from a structural burden into a dynamic stabilizer, achieving structural value stacking.

WTGES exhibits unique mechanical nonlinear characteristics in frequency support performance. We find that the inertial support effect of GES couples highly with the directionality of wind speed fluctuations. In scenarios of overall wind speed decline (power deficit), the discharging mode, through synergy of potential energy release and motor inertia, shows superior frequency extremum suppression compared to the charging mode. In contrast, wind speed increase scenarios reverse this result. This asymmetry strongly demonstrates the unidirectional nature of inertia support in GES systems. Additionally, WTGES performs slightly inferior on frequency RMS metrics compared to responsive electrochemical storage. This stems from jerk limits and physical delays of the mechanical system. This characteristic clearly defines the strategic positioning of WTGES. It serves as a “grid safety airbag” to provide robust support against large deviations and low-frequency drops. This positioning is quantitatively supported by our global potential assessment (Supplementary Note 7). The stark contrast between the high inertial power potential (~4.8 GW)—equivalent to the inertia of 7–14 large coal-fired power plants—and the limited energy capacity ( ~ 0.25 GWh) suggests that WTGES is optimally deployed for high-power, short-duration ancillary services. Thus, it leverages the robustness advantage of mechanical inertia under high-current impacts, rather than for precise smoothing of minor power fluctuations.

Although the LCOS of WTGES is much higher than that of lithium batteries, it offers cross-order-of-magnitude advantages in power density and asset lifespan. By apportioning the mass block costs between structural protection (OPEX reduction) and ancillary services (revenue increase), the value stacking framework we propose corrects the underestimation of GES in traditional models. Moreover, WTGES reuses existing tower infrastructure, thereby eliminating high civil engineering costs in its initial investment. Projected OPEX savings from the TMD effect also theoretically account for approximately 20-30% of the integrated system’s gross annual revenus (including baseline wind electricity sales). Lifecycle NPV comparisons indicate that WTGES can exhibit a competitive revenue curve, as it avoids the mandatory retirement replacement required for battery systems. Consequently, this positions WTGES as a potentially attractive alternative to electrochemical storage for ultra-long-cycle asset operations.

The deployment of WTGES aligns highly with multiple United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). In terms of resilience and disaster reduction (SDG 11 and 13), it aligns with the United Nations Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction. Thus, the system enhances wind farm resilience under extreme climates through the TMD effect. Moreover, it assists in wind power grid integration to reduce system peaking pressure. In terms of circular economy and resource reuse (SDG 12), under reasonable conditions, we suggest utilizing/recycling retired wind turbine blades to prepare masses. In addition, we propose deploying GES using height differences in old turbine towers. This achieves “re-industrialization” of waste infrastructure and avoids resource waste. Our assessment indicates that selectively retrofitting Direct-Drive (PMSG) fleets and repurposing end-of-life assets offers a theoretical technical upper bound of ~200 GW for global hosting capacity. Based on this, regulatory agencies should design differentiated subsidy mechanisms according to the physical characteristics of energy storage technologies. They should establish specialized “high-lifespan inertia service” entry standards for technologies like WTGES with dual “structural + grid” attributes. In policy design, the social value of mitigating structural fatigue should be capitalized. Thus, it incentivizes developers to synchronously integrate TMD storage modules in ultra-large offshore wind planning.

Although simulations rigorously validate the synergy mechanism, acknowledging the system’s boundary conditions clarifies its practical deployment pathway. First, regarding structural fatigue, the ~50-fold life extension from Miner’s rule marks a theoretical upper bound for structural fatigue. In real-world environments, complex multi-directional aerodynamic loads and higher-order modal coupling will inevitably attenuate the actual fatigue gains. Nevertheless, the profound mitigation of primary dynamic loads confirms a definitive resilience upgrade over baseline towers. Second, WTGES inherently delivers half-directional inertia. While this necessitates coordination with other fast-responding assets (e.g., batteries) during rapidly alternating frequency disturbances, it demonstrates robust capability in arresting severe, unidirectional frequency drops, which often represent the most critical threat to grid stability. Third, high-cycle operation causes mechanical wear on cables and dampers. Yet, by adapting mature, heavy-duty components from the mining hoist industry, these maintenance demands are highly predictable and can be embedded within standard wind farm servicing cycles. Finally, fully monetizing the structural OPEX savings depends on the evolution of future power market designs. Still, as demonstrated in the lifecycle NPV analysis, the system’s ability to avoid the mandatory decadal replacement costs associated with electrochemical batteries secures its economic competitiveness, specifically for high-frequency power regulation. To address these limits, future work should progress to megawatt-scale field prototyping to empirically quantify long-term mechanical wear and multi-axial fatigue under real weather conditions. Furthermore, developing hybrid control frameworks that explicitly coordinate WTGES with electrochemical storage will be crucial for providing seamless, full-quadrant grid support. Ultimately, by upgrading conventional wind turbine towers into multifunctional grid-stabilizing assets, WTGES offers a pragmatic and synergistic evolution for future deep-offshore wind infrastructure.

A defining characteristic of the rope-driven WTGES is its “Directional Asymmetry” or “Half-Directional Inertia.” Unlike a solid shaft that transmits torque bidirectionally, the flexible cables can only transmit tension, not compression. This creates a mode-dependent inertial response: In Discharging Mode (Mass Descending): The system provides effective inertial support for under-frequency events (\(\Delta f < 0\)). The descending mass releases gravitational potential and kinetic energy to counter the frequency drop. However, it cannot effectively absorb energy to counter a frequency rise (\(\Delta f > 0\)) as the rope cannot push the mass down. In Charging Mode (Mass Ascending): The system provides effective inertial support for over-frequency events (\(\Delta f > 0\)). The inertia of the rising mass resists acceleration, acting as a brake to absorb excess grid power. Conversely, during a frequency drop (\(\Delta f < 0\)), the mass’s kinetic energy is largely consumed by gravity rather than being fed back to the grid. This physical nonlinearity means the WTGES functions as a “conditional” inertial buffer, providing varying degrees of support depending on the alignment between the grid disturbance direction and the mass’s kinematic state.

Multi-scale simulation setup and hierarchical control

To rigorously validate the scalability of the WTGES and its grid-support efficacy across different industrial scenarios, we established a multi-scale simulation framework comprising three independent physical models and one farm-level cluster. Independent physical modeling across scales: We developed high-fidelity dynamic models for three distinct turbine classes, rather than relying on linear mathematical extrapolation. 300 kW Microgrid Prototype: Serves as the baseline for verifying fundamental inertial response mechanisms and control logic in low-inertia environments. 3.4 MW Onshore Mainstream Turbine: Configured according to the IEA Wind Task 37 Reference Wind Turbine specifications, representing the current standard for land-based assets. 10 MW Offshore Future Turbine: Based on the IEA/DTU reference standards for next-generation deep-sea applications, specifically designed to evaluate stability under high wind speeds and flexible tower conditions. The detailed geometric, mass, and drivetrain parameters for each class are strictly anchored in industrial standards and are provided in Supplementary Table 1. To evaluate grid-level interactions, we constructed a 101 MW onshore wind farm model consisting of 30 units of 3.4 MW turbines. The cluster adopts a standard 5-row × 6-column rectangular matrix layout. To isolate electrical frequency responses from aerodynamic wake losses in this specific study, the turbine spacing is set to 15D (cross-wind) and 20D (along-wind), where D is the rotor diameter. This spacing effectively minimizes wake interference, allowing the cluster to be modeled with uniform wind input for frequency stability analysis. To ensure simulation fidelity under stochastic field conditions, idealized step inputs were replaced with high-frequency field-measured wind speed data. We utilized the Björkö Island dataset (sampled at 100 Hz), ensuring that the system’s dynamic response—particularly the active damping and power smoothing—is tested against realistic turbulence spectra rather than simplified profiles. The hybrid system employs a hierarchical control architecture to manage the multi-physics interaction between the turbine, the gravity mass, and the grid: The turbine operates under a Variable Speed Variable Pitch (VSVP) framework. At low wind speeds, a Hill Climbing Search (HCS) based Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) algorithm optimizes energy capture. The grid interface is managed by a full-scale back-to-back Voltage Source Converter (VSC) utilizing Space Vector Pulse Width Modulation (SVPWM), which decouples active and reactive power control to maintain high power quality. The gravity storage unit operates on a “Dual-Layer Mechanism.” On the macro layer, it follows grid dispatch commands (e.g., peak shifting) for energy management. On the micro layer, it provides “Intrinsic Mechanical Inertia” via the physical coupling of the rotating motor and suspended mass. Unlike synthetic inertia that requires frequency derivative calculation, this support is physically inherent and active by default, acting as an immediate buffer against frequency excursions. For structural protection, the active damping loop modulates the mass motion to counteract tower vibrations based on real-time acceleration feedback (see “Structural dynamics” section).

Hierarchical control and safety prioritization strategy

To fully resolve potential conflicts between grid-support objectives and structural safety demands under varying aerodynamic loads, the WTGES control system implements a deterministic, three-tier priority decoupling strategy governed by strict environmental thresholds. First, under standard wind conditions, the system prioritizes grid support and operates in energy storage mode. In this normal operational regime, the dynamic bandwidth of grid frequency regulation is kinematically separated from the tower’s primary structural natural frequency. This bandwidth separation fundamentally avoids resonant excitation, allowing the system to safely execute active power injection and absorption. Second, when wind speeds approach rated limits or turbulent intensity increases, structural damping takes precedence as mitigating dynamic fatigue becomes paramount. Consequently, all grid-support operations are explicitly suspended. The suspended mass is engaged exclusively as a passive TMD at an optimal height, oscillating to dissipate horizontal vibrational energy and significantly reducing both RMS displacement and drivetrain acceleration (as demonstrated in Fig. 3a, b). Finally, a fail-safe survival priority is enacted during extreme weather events, such as a 50-year EOG where wind speeds exceed cut-out thresholds. In this regime, the primary threat shifts from dynamic fatigue to ultimate static failure (overturning), making the TMD’s dynamic absorption insufficient against extreme unidirectional deflection. To counter this, a hardware-level mechanism is triggered: the mass is decoupled, rapidly lowered, and mechanically locked to the tower base (Fig. 3f). This critical intervention instantaneously lowers the system’s center of gravity and eliminates the massive secondary bending moment induced by the suspended weight, thereby preventing the catastrophic amplification of P-Delta effects. Ultimately, this hard-boundary state-machine precisely maps control actions to specific physical threats (grid instability, dynamic fatigue, and static overturning), ensuring that the turbine’s structural integrity is never compromised across any operational or survival regime.

To avoid underestimating engineering costs, the initial capital expenditure (\({{\boldsymbol{C}}}_{{\boldsymbol{inc}}}\)) is estimated using a “Bottom-Up Cost Model” rather than generic percentages. The cost boundary strictly includes not only the core energy conversion hardware (motor/generator, power electronics) and the mass block, but also the “Structural Integration Subsystem.” This subsystem explicitly accounts for high-strength steel wire ropes (derived from mining hoist standards), hydraulic viscous dampers for active vibration control, guide rail assemblies, and localized tower reinforcements. Detailed unit prices and component breakdowns based on industrial benchmarks are provided in Supplementary Tables 9–11.

$${NPV}=-{C}_{{inc}}+\mathop{\sum }\limits_{t=1}^{N}\frac{{R}_{{freq},\,t}+{R}_{{inertia},\,t}+{R}_{{saving},\,t}-{C}_{O{\& }M,\,t}}{{\left(1+r\right)}^{t}}-\frac{{C}_{{Rep}}}{{\left(1+r\right)}^{10}}$$

(13)

$${LCOS}=\frac{{C}_{{inc}}+{\sum }_{t=1}^{N}\frac{{C}_{O\& M,\,t}+{C}_{{Rep}}}{{\left(1+r\right)}^{t}}}{{\sum }_{t=1}^{N}\frac{{E}_{{nom}}{D}_{{cyc}}{\eta }_{{sys}}}{{\left(1+r\right)}^{t}}}$$

(14)

Global technical potential estimation

To quantify the macro-scale grid support capability of WTGES and avoid the overestimation bias inherent in uniform penetration models, we developed a bottom-up “Multidimensional Technical Filter Model.” This model screens the global wind asset database (anchored in the 2023 cumulative capacity of 1021 GW reported by GWEC) through three strict engineering constraints: We restrict the addressable retrofit market strictly to Direct-Drive (PMSG) turbines. Unlike geared systems, PMSG architectures feature a large-diameter hollow shaft that allows vertical cable routing through the nacelle center, thereby eliminating the risk of eccentric structural loading. Based on industry statistical ranges, we define the PMSG share in the existing global fleet as 27.5%. To ensure structural safety margins, we exclude aging turbines with a rated power below 2 MW. For the remaining addressable PMSG stock, we apply a conservative “Structural Suitability Factor” of 50% to account for specific geometric constraints that may prevent retrofitting. Consequently, the retrofit potential from the existing fleet is calculated with Eq. 15, where \({{\boldsymbol{C}}}_{{\bf{total}}}\) is the global cumulative capacity. For new offshore installations (projected 300 GW by 2030), we apply a higher PMSG market share of 68% and assume a 30% “Design-Phase Integration Rate,” reflecting the higher feasibility of incorporating WTGES during the initial turbine design rather than retrofitting. The Total Hosting Capacity is the sum of the retrofit and new integration segments. The global Effective Inertial Power and Energy Storage Capacity are derived by mapping the unit-level benchmarks (from the 3.4 and 10 MW simulation models described in “Methods—Multi-scale simulation setup and hierarchical control”) to this aggregated capacity. Sensitivity analysis is performed by varying the PMSG share and adoption rates by \(\pm {\bf{10}} \%\) to define the uncertainty boundaries.

$${C}_{{\rm{retrofit}}}={C}_{{\rm{total}}}\times 0.275{C}_{{\rm{PMSG}}}\times 0.5{C}_{{\rm{suitability}}}$$

(15)

Evaluation metrics

To comprehensively quantify the system’s inertial support capability and stability performance under disturbances, we adopt two primary frequency-domain metrics. Frequency Standard Deviation (\({{\boldsymbol{\sigma }}}_{{\bf{f}}}\)) characterizes the overall amplitude of frequency oscillations throughout the disturbance window, as shown in Eq. 16, where \({\boldsymbol{f}}\left({{\boldsymbol{t}}}_{{\boldsymbol{i}}}\right)\) is the instantaneous grid frequency at sampling time \({{\boldsymbol{t}}}_{{\boldsymbol{i}}}\), \(\bar{{\boldsymbol{f}}}\) is the mean frequency, and \({\boldsymbol{N}}\) is the total number of samples. A lower \({{\boldsymbol{\sigma }}}_{{\bf{f}}}\) indicates effective damping of sustained oscillations. Maximum Frequency Deviation (\(\Delta {{\boldsymbol{f}}}_{{\bf{\max }}}\)), calculated with Eq. 17, captures the peak transient severity immediately following a power imbalance (e.g., at the frequency nadir or zenith), where \({{\boldsymbol{f}}}_{{\bf{0}}}\) is the nominal grid frequency (50 Hz) and \({{\boldsymbol{t}}}_{{\bf{0}}}\) is the disturbance onset time. While the RoCoF is a standard indicator for inertia, \(\Delta {{\boldsymbol{f}}}_{{\bf{\max }}}\) provides a more direct measure of the system’s ability to arrest frequency excursions within safe operating limits, particularly for capacity-constrained storage systems.

$${\sigma }_{{\rm{f}}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i=1}^{N}{\left[f\left({t}_{i}\right)-\bar{f}\right]}^{2}}$$

(16)

$$\Delta {f}_{\max }=\mathop{\max }\limits_{t\ge {t}_{0}}\left|f\left(t\right)-{f}_{0}\right|$$

title: Natural Gas Predicted to Surpass Oil as America's Primary Energy by 2030 - Briefs Finance
description:
By 2030, natural gas is expected to surpass oil - not because oil use is falling fast, but because gas keeps winning in power generation while oil demand nearly flatlines.
Starting in the early 2000s, the shale revolution reshaped American energy by unlocking vast natural gas reserves that became profitable to extract.
The Energy Information Administration projects U.S. natural gas demand will rise 3.4% from 2025 to 2027, while petroleum demand edges up just 0.6%.
Between 2015 and 2025, the use of wind and solar energy increased more than threefold, whereas natural gas consumption grew by 23%, despite natural gas seeing larger absolute gains.
What to Watch Wind and solar are growing faster in percentage terms, but natural gas remains the largest power-plant fuel by a wide margin.
text:
For 75 years, petroleum has been the predominant U.S. energy source. That's about to change. By 2030, natural gas is expected to surpass oil - not because oil use is falling fast, but because gas keeps winning in power generation while oil demand nearly flatlines.

Coal's share of U.S. electricity generation has fallen from roughly 50% in 2000 to under 20% today, as natural gas and renewables have taken over. This trend is expected to continue despite political support for coal.

This transition represents a fundamental shift in the nation's energy mix, as oil has dominated since the 1950s, fueling transportation and industry. Natural gas, once considered a waste product, now powers homes, factories, and power plants across the country.

Starting in the early 2000s, the shale revolution reshaped American energy by unlocking vast natural gas reserves that became profitable to extract. This abundance drove down prices and made natural gas the preferred fuel for new power plants, displacing coal and competing with oil. Ira Joseph, a researcher at Columbia University's global energy policy center, said, "Gas "is dominant in power because it's so inexpensive". "There's just plentiful amounts of natural gas in this country"."

Meanwhile, U.S. gasoline demand has flattened as electric vehicles cut into oil's traditional base. Growing electricity needs from data centers and EVs are boosting demand for gas-fired power. The Energy Information Administration projects U.S. natural gas demand will rise 3.4% from 2025 to 2027, while petroleum demand edges up just 0.6%.

Get your free investing masterclass bonus when you join Market Briefs, our free daily newsletter

That shift is visible in the electricity market. Between 2015 and 2025, the use of wind and solar energy increased more than threefold, whereas natural gas consumption grew by 23%, despite natural gas seeing larger absolute gains.

What the Data Says

Toby Rice, CEO of EQT Corp., expects the crossover soon. "I say we probably cross that threshold within the next couple years, and by 2030, we will have a big lead on petroleum," Rice said.

The government's own forecasts support that view. Coal is still declining despite hundreds of millions of taxpayer dollars allocated by President Donald Trump to support the industry. One source simply outcompetes the other on cost.

The LNG Boom

Natural gas isn't just winning at home. Shell predicts U.S. feedgas for LNG plants will make up 23% of total U.S. gas production by 2035, according to its annual LNG outlook.

As Ira Joseph noted, the economics are straightforward: cheap domestic supply meets rising global demand.

What to Watch

Wind and solar are growing faster in percentage terms, but natural gas remains the largest power-plant fuel by a wide margin. Mark Brownstein, the Environmental Defense Fund's senior vice president of energy transition, summed it up: "The facts don't lie: The United States is in the midst of an energy transition, away from coal and oil, toward electricity produced by natural gas and renewables."

For investors, the trend is clear. Toby Rice put it in historical context: "We've gone from the age of wood and horses to the age of coal to the age of petroleum, and now we are in the age of electrification. "And the age of electrification is going to be driven a lot by natural gas"."

text:
Families and businesses will continue to reap the benefits of the clean energy transition in the coming decades, as Britain steps up action to get off the fossil fuel rollercoaster

Government sets next achievable and pragmatic target for long-term emissions reduction, building on the framework that has secured billions of private investment and economic growth since 2008, a “great British success story”

Moving at pace to electrify Britain and deliver clean, homegrown energy will unlock greater energy security, lower bills for good, cleaner air, thousands of good jobs and action on the climate crisis following record British heatwaves

Families and businesses across the UK will continue to reap the benefits of the clean energy transition, as the government sets a new emissions target to further protect family finances, grow the economy and tackle the climate crisis.

As Britain faces its second fossil fuel price shock in 5 years due to the war in Iran, the government is pursuing policies which deliver tangible improvements to the lives of working people - centred on getting Britain off the rollercoaster of fossil fuel markets and onto clean homegrown power.

Today (Tuesday 2 June) the government has set out its proposed level for the seventh Carbon Budget, which sets a science-led target of ~87% emissions reduction in the period 2038 to 2042 – endorsed by the Environmental Audit Committee and the Climate Change Committee.

It comes as an independent report from the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, supported by analysis from the Confederation of British Industries Economics, today shows that the net zero economy supports over one million jobs in the UK, adding £105 billion in gross value added (GVA) to the UK economy in 2025 alone, as it continues to thrive as one of the UK’s fastest- growing economic sectors.

The new target is based on evidence-based assumptions about how the country will take a consumer choice-led approach to the adoption of technologies such as solar, batteries and EVs that will cut bills for families.

The level for the Seventh Carbon Budget has been chosen because:

moving at pace to clean energy and net zero emissions is the best choice to reduce the exposure of UK families and businesses to more fossil fuel shocks, as the UK has seen following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the Iran War

it maximises the benefits of the clean energy and net zero transition, including to the economy, health and nature

it is consistent with the Paris Agreement aim to keep global warming to 1.5 degrees, to avoid climate disaster for future generations

This builds on the UK’s pioneering Climate Change Act 2008 - backed by British businesses, scientists, trade unions and civil society - which has provided a framework for combining economic growth and climate action, attracting billions of private sector investment and seen the UK become a global leader in clean energy industries. Since July 2024, the UK has seen over £90 billion of private investment announced in clean energy, including carbon capture projects in Teesside and nuclear at Sizewell C off the Suffolk coast.

The government’s clean energy and climate plans include:

Cutting bills and costs: March saw the highest monthly solar deployment in over a decade and a record month for EV sales. Families installing solar could save up to £500 a year, electric cars can save drivers up to £1,400 annually to run and external estimates show new electric cars are now on average, cheaper to buy than petrol equivalents. Alongside this, the £15 billion Warm Homes Plan will deliver the biggest home upgrade programme in British history, cutting bills and lifting millions out of fuel poverty

Delivering energy security: Half of the UK’s recessions since 1970 have been caused by fossil fuel shocks. The government is investing in renewable and nuclear energy to get the UK off the rollercoaster of fossil fuel prices, delivering a record-breaking renewables auction that secured enough clean energy to power the equivalent of 23 million homes. By 2050, the UK could cut its reliance on fossil fuels from around three quarters of our energy today to around 15%, while avoiding around £445 billion in fossil fuel spending over the next 25 years

Jobs and investment: The government is driving a major clean energy jobs push, supporting over 400,000 additional jobs by 2030 across the UK. According to the CBI Economics report, in 2025, jobs supported by net zero businesses were 48%, or 1.5 times more productive than the UK average, generating £119,300 in economic value per full-time job. This led to higher-than-average wages, with these jobs generating an average of £43,142 to a full-time worker

Cleaner air and nature recovery: Clean energy will help make the air cleaner across the country, leading to better health and a higher quality of life for people now and in the future. Cleaner air from the transition is estimated to deliver around 8,000 fewer hospital admissions each year by 2050, easing pressure on the NHS. Restoring peatlands and planting new woodland will deliver around £50 billion in nature benefits over the period to 2050, improving biodiversity, water quality, flood protection and access to nature

Without action, climate change continues to endanger the UK’s food and water security, exacerbate global population displacement and pose national security risks, including to critical infrastructure, in a context of increased global instability and households already suffering from the price volatility of fossil fuels. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) is also clear that the costs of climate damage are getting higher, while the cost of the net zero transition is getting lower. This is about protecting the UK’s way of life and the natural world from significant dangers.

Energy Secretary Ed Miliband said: 'As Britain faces the second fossil fuel shock of the decade, the only way to protect family and business finances is to drive for clean homegrown power that we control. What has been achieved so far by businesses and communities across the country is a great British success story - cutting costs by upgrading homes, backing British businesses, supporting one million good jobs according to new analysis from CBI Economics, and protecting our beautiful countryside. Some people want to stick their heads in the sand and let our children face the consequences of climate breakdown - but this government believes in the timeless British value of protecting our country for generations to come.'

Climate Minister Katie White said: 'The record-breaking May heatwave is another reminder that climate change is no longer a distant prospect. Increased heatwaves, flooding and nature loss are becoming the new norm for our country. That’s why we’re continuing to set a clear investment framework which will electrify Britain, maximising the benefits of clean power with cleaner air, warmer homes, energy security, investment into Britain and thousands of jobs in the industries of the future.'

A delivery plan setting out how Carbon Budget 7 will be met will be published as soon as is reasonably practical after Parliament has approved the budget.

Legislating the carbon budget level for 2038 to 2042 now sends an economy-wide signal to investors and businesses, providing long-term certainty which will encourage investment and growth.

text:
Dozens of natural gas power plants planned across the state to fuel data centers could emit more greenhouse gases than every household in Texas – combined.

That’s according to a new report by the Environmental Integrity Project, a nonprofit focused on enforcement of environmental laws, which tracked 74 gas-powered plants in development across the country as dedicated sources of electricity for data centers.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

READ MORE: Greg Abbott calls for prohibition on data center construction in rural Texas neighborhoods

Nearly half are in Texas, which is on track to be the world’s largest data center hub. These plants could emit more than 287 million tons of greenhouse gases annually, the report found – roughly the equivalent of 61 million gas-powered cars driven for a year.

Researchers at EIP scoured state permit applications, data center tracking websites, and industry publications to identify so-called “behind-the-meter” plants that bypass the grid to connect directly to data centers.

According to plans submitted or published by companies, these power plants are expected to generate roughly 63 gigawatts of energy – enough to power the entire state of Texas on a normal spring day.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

As the state’s grid operator, ERCOT, grapples with an enormous backlog of massive energy requests, data center developers have increasingly turned to on-site power generation as a way to get online more quickly.

State leaders as well as President Donald Trump have encouraged behind-the-meter power production as a way to minimize rate increases for local households and avoid strain on grid operators.

But because companies are mostly turning to natural gas to power data center operations, these plants will significantly increase greenhouse gas emissions and emit air pollutants linked to respiratory illnesses and heart disease.

“The potential public health and environmental impacts we found, even from this small slice of the industry, is alarming,” said Jen Duggan, EIP’s executive director.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The group is advocating for data centers to be powered by clean energy, including solar farms and wind turbines. “It makes no sense for a technology of the future to be powered by the dirty fossil fuels of the past,” Duggan said.

The largest behind-the-meter power plant planned in Texas is Project Matador by Fermi America, the company cofounded by former Texas Gov. Rick Perry, which will provide up to 17 gigawatts of electricity for a proposed 18-million-square-foot data center outside Amarillo.

“That's enough power for New York City, while we have neighbors who rely on church donations to catch up on their electric bills,” said Kendra Seawright, an organizer with Panhandle 1st Coalition, a grassroots group fighting the Fermi America project.

One project in West Texas, the Pecos Power Generation facility, applied for funding from the Texas Energy Fund, which supplies grants and loans to new gas-fired power plants, provided that a majority of the plant’s electricity goes to the grid.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Shop Spurs Gear

Neither company responded immediately to a request for comment.

Roughly half of the plants identified in the report had submitted applications for Clean Air Act construction permits, said Griffin Bird, a researcher at EIP and the report’s lead author. Those applications include preliminary emissions estimates. For plants that hadn’t applied for permits, researchers estimated emissions from the planned natural gas-fired turbines and engines.

Amy Margolies, the executive director of Tucker United, a grassroots group opposing a West Virginia data center, noted in a press conference on the report that behind-the-meter power plants can avoid the regulatory scrutiny required of plants connecting to the grid. “Off the grid can be off the rails,” she said.

title: Champaign County seeking legal counsel to regulate data centers following failure of Illinois ...
authors: Makenna Norman / For CU-CitizenAccess, Makenna Norman, For CU-CitizenAccess
description:

text:
The failure to pass a proposed state law on data centers has pushed Champaign County officials to develop their own regulations to address concerns about the centers’ water consumption, noise pollution and rising energy costs.

The Illinois POWER Act would have been one of the few state regulations on data center operations and would’ve forced data centers to pay the total cost of the energy usage, rather than letting those costs fall on households and local businesses. However, the Act failed to advance in the Illinois General Assembly on June 1.

Emily Rodriguez, vice chair of the County Board and chair of the Data Center Activities Task Force, said the lack of state legislation means counties will have a harder time enforcing certain regulations against data centers.

“The state legislature failed to pass any sort of data center regulation … so by the state constitution, we can’t do much to protect ourselves from data centers,” Rodriguez said in an interview with CU-CitizenAccess.org. “Requiring data centers to pay for their own energy and infrastructure, requiring certain safety standards for water and water usage — these are all things that we would have a hard time enforcing, but the state absolutely can.”

The issue of data centers in the county arose earlier this year when officials said there had been an approach by developers about the possibility of a data center on a 300-acre area located in the southwest section of the City of Champaign. City and task force officials have refused to identify the developer or the location because they said they have not received an official proposal.

Large data centers are being constructed in Illinois and neighboring states like Indiana.

Construction began this year in Lebanon, Ind. on a Meta 1,500-acre data center campus with a capacity to use 1 gigawatt of power, compared to traditional data centers that typically use up to 100 megawatts. In Yorkville, Ill., a 1,037-acre data center campus was approved by city officials, but residents filed a lawsuit to try to block the construction.

On June 22, the task force met for its fifth meeting as the eight committee members continued to draft an ordinance on data center regulations. The ordinance will dictate policies that future data centers built in Champaign County must abide by should any be approved after the 12-month moratorium ends in April 2027.

The task force primarily discussed energy regulations at the June 22 meeting because of data centers’ significant strain on the power grid and how average consumers rates tend to rise to accommodate nearby data centers.

“I think we can get more renewable [energy sources] built out so we can ensure data centers in Champaign are doing their part,” said Andrew Rehn, task force member and director of climate policy at Prairie Rivers Network, during the meeting. “The [language] we are using in the POWER Act is ‘bring your own new clean capacity and energy,’ and that doesn’t have to be on-site.”

The task force discussed renewable energy mandates for data centers, including the benefits of renewable energy to prevent high power costs for consumers and the potential downsides, such as new solar or wind farms being built over farmland.

“I attended a meeting at the Farm Bureau this past winter, and the view there was that ‘bring your own clean energy’ is just going to use up more of the best prime farmland for solar arrays,” County Planning and Zoning Director John Hall said during the June 22 meeting.

The drafted ordinance additionally bans the use of nuclear power. After some discussion on whether changes should be made in the case that modular nuclear reactors advance to be an effective energy source for data centers, the task force decided to keep the ban on nuclear reactors in the draft, a provision that can be requested to be waived like all other requirements in the ordinance.

“It’s one of the benefits of public policy,” Rodriguez said during the meeting. “It can be amended, it can be changed as time changes [and] community needs change.”

Water preservation, noise and energy costs drive local concerns

Previously, at the task force’s June 1 meeting, water use regulations was the main point of discussion. Many data centers use evaporative cooling measures, which extracts water from lakes, rivers and groundwater sources and uses the evaporation process to cool the heat generated by data centers’ extreme energy usage.

Evaporative cooling requires continuous water extraction, thus the task force is considering enforcing systems such as closed-loop cooling, which is able to reuse the same water and therefore prevent continuous water extraction from the Mahomet Aquifer.

“We know [the aquifer] is a finite resource, and that if we overdraw the aquifer, communities that are dependent on it will suffer,” Rehn said in an interview with CU-CitizenAccess. “We’re at the top of a watershed, so we’re deeply dependent on the resource, and so we just need to be thoughtful about when a large water user, like a data center, shows up, and what sort of restrictions we want to put in place.”

The task force plans to tackle in future meetings issues of noise and vibration caused by large data centers. The humming of cooling systems, generators and fans can be heard up to a mile away, and the extremely low frequencies can be felt similarly to the vibration of bass-heavy music at a concert.

As the task force continues drafting regulation for data centers, members have been using the Aurora, Ill. ordinance as a guideline. Aurora passed strict data center regulations in March after a 180-day long moratorium, similar to Champaign’s current 12-month moratorium on data centers, with strict policies on noise, water consumption and energy usage.

At the task force’s May 4 meeting, members were joined via video call by City of Aurora Mayor John Laesch and Director of Sustainability Alison Lindburg to discuss Aurora’s regulations and the city’s decision-making process.

Although the task force has been considering Aurora’s regulations as a blueprint, a major difference between Aurora and Champaign is that Aurora is a home rule municipality, meaning it has the power to self-govern and pass its own local laws unless specifically prohibited by the state. Champaign is a non-home rule municipality, meaning it may only exercise powers expressly granted by state law.

“A lot of the Aurora [ordinance] we cannot do. We can definitely use it as a framework, but there are going to be large chunks where the answer is just ‘no, we can’t require that. We have no authority,’” said Champaign County Executive Michelle Jett during the May 4 meeting.

Aurora’s ordinance includes the provision to fine data centers $1,000 to 5,000 a day per violation, an authority it has as a home-rule municipality. The state limits Champaign to fines of up to $500 which must be imposed by a court — a price that data centers may potentially disregard as the cost of doing business.

“We are capped by the state on what we can do and, frankly, there are dollar amounts that these large data centers would laugh at,” Jett said during the June 22 meeting

Task force consulting with attorney on county’s authority

Task Force chair Rodriguez said during the June 22 meeting that the task force will be meeting with an attorney to ask questions regarding Champaign’s authority as a non-home rule county.

“We’re waiting for something in writing from the State’s Attorney’s Office,” Rodriguez said in an interview with CU-CitizenAccess. “It would have been inappropriate to guess [the county’s enforcement ability] … so we’re going to have to delay any serious consideration until we hear something from the State’s Attorney’s Office, and I think they’re rounding that corner soon.”

A Champaign County Board Meeting on April 23 to discuss the length of the moratorium had a large public turnout with several citizens speaking over the span of the two-hour meeting and a majority of speakers expressing their desire to keep data centers out of Champaign.

However, as emphasized by Jett in the public task force meetings, and by Rodriguez in an interview, the county does not have the authority to outright ban data centers. State statutes do not explicitly authorize non-home rule counties to prohibit legitimate, permitted business operations.

“Legally, we could be sued if we take a stance that is full, no data centers,” Rodriguez said. “It’s a power thing that data centers have. We have to pass something that’s reasonable, that stands for our community, but it’s not a yes or no question, and it never will be.”

Rodriguez said no data center company propositioned Champaign for a potential data center location, but a construction company responsible for building data centers scouted locations in the county. No official proposals have been made.

“We’re seeing [data centers] in other counties, and [have been] dissatisfied with the process by which we’re seeing these ordinances passed and projects approved,” Rodriguez said. “So [we’re] being proactive, we don’t have any serious proposals, though. And I want to be really clear about that. We met with a data center builder who just kind of wanted to get a sense of Champaign County, but there were no proposals on where and how.”

name: American Energy
title: Resilient, reliable, sustainable: Q-and-A with Vince Weatherstein, Miami's director of Energy Systems
description:
Throughout my career, I've worked with steam plants, electrical generation systems, chilled water systems, and campus utility distribution networks.
In industry, energy systems are typically designed around a single process or product.
Our goal is to provide safe, reliable, resilient, and sustainable energy systems that support Miami's mission while being responsible stewards of the university's resources.
As new facilities are planned, energy systems are being evaluated early in the design process to maximize efficiency and sustainability.
Energy systems are often behind the scenes, but they are critical to everything the university does.
text:
What drew you to this position at Miami?

Weatherstein: The opportunity to lead a diverse and complex utility portfolio while making a meaningful impact on the university's long-term energy strategy. Miami has demonstrated a commitment to reliability, sustainability, and infrastructure investment through initiatives such as geothermal expansion, renewable energy projects, and utility modernization. Those priorities aligned well with my background and interests.

Most importantly, I saw an opportunity to build a strong team, improve reliability and efficiency, and help position the university for future energy challenges. Being able to contribute to an institution whose mission is education while leading critical infrastructure that supports students, faculty, and staff made the role particularly appealing.

What is your background in the energy industry, and what are some of the changes you’ve seen in the industry?

Weatherstein: My background in the energy industry has been primarily focused on utility generation, distribution, and energy management. Throughout my career, I've worked with steam plants, electrical generation systems, chilled water systems, and campus utility distribution networks. I've had the opportunity to lead operations, maintenance, capital projects, and strategic planning efforts while ensuring reliable utility service to critical facilities.

One of the biggest changes I've seen in the industry is the shift from a sole focus on reliability and production to balancing reliability, sustainability, efficiency, and resiliency. Years ago, success was often measured simply by whether the lights stayed on and the heat kept running. Today, organizations are also expected to reduce carbon emissions, improve energy efficiency, integrate renewable resources, and leverage advanced controls and analytics to optimize operations.

A campus energy system differs significantly from an industrial facility. In industry, energy systems are typically designed around a single process or product. On a university campus, the utility infrastructure supports a wide variety of building types and users: classrooms, laboratories, residence halls, dining facilities, athletic venues, and research spaces, each with unique operating requirements.

What would you like the Miami community to know about energy systems on campus?

Weatherstein: The energy systems that support campus don't happen by accident. The heat in the winter, air conditioning in the summer, electricity, hot water, and the infrastructure that supports research and learning are all the result of decades of planning, investment, and dedicated work by many individuals.

Much of what we do is intentionally invisible. When our systems are operating as designed, most people never think about them and that's actually a sign of success. Behind the scenes, there are teams of professionals operating and maintaining hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of critical infrastructure 24 hours a day, 365 days a year.

Many of the projects we are implementing today were envisioned and planned years ago by leaders and staff who understood the importance of investing in the university's future. My predecessors and the teams that came before us laid the foundation for much of the progress we are seeing today, and they deserve tremendous credit for their vision, planning, and persistence.

The decisions being made today are not just for the next year or two; they are investments that will impact the campus for decades. Our goal is to provide safe, reliable, resilient, and sustainable energy systems that support Miami's mission while being responsible stewards of the university's resources.

After completion of the solar arrays and the North Geothermal Project this year, what are some upcoming projects toward decarbonizing our Oxford campus energy systems ?

Weatherstein: One of the most impactful upcoming initiatives is the continued conversion of the campus heating distribution system from steam to heating hot water (HHW). This transition improves overall system efficiency, reduces distribution losses, lowers maintenance requirements, and creates opportunities to integrate renewable and low-carbon heating technologies in the future. Several buildings, including Armstrong Student Center, Warfield Hall, and MacMillan Hall, are currently being converted as part of this effort.

We are also advancing plans to expand our geothermal infrastructure to support future campus growth. As new facilities are planned, energy systems are being evaluated early in the design process to maximize efficiency and sustainability. The proposed multipurpose arena, for example, is planned to be connected to the campus geothermal loop.

Looking further ahead, we are continuing to develop plans for Phase 1 of the Steam Plant Transformation Project. While still several years away, this project represents a major milestone in Miami's decarbonization journey. The long-term vision is to transition from a centralized steam generation system to a modern heating hot water-based energy system, positioning the university to leverage geothermal, heat recovery, and other emerging technologies while maintaining the reliability and resilience required to support campus operations.

What is one of your favorite things about working at Miami?

Weatherstein: One of my favorite things about working at Miami is the opportunity to make a visible impact on the campus every day. Energy systems are often behind the scenes, but they are critical to everything the university does. Whether it's providing heat during the winter, cooling during the summer, supporting research laboratories, or ensuring students have a comfortable place to learn and live, our work touches every part of the campus.

I also enjoy the variety that comes with working in energy systems. No two days are exactly alike. One day I may be working on a long-term infrastructure project such as geothermal expansion or utility modernization, and the next I may be focused on operational challenges, reliability improvements, or supporting the team through an outage or emergency response.

Most importantly, I enjoy working with the people. We have a highly skilled team with decades of experience, and there is a strong sense of pride in what we do. Watching the team solve problems, adapt to new technologies, and continue improving our systems is extremely rewarding.

Energy systems are the backbone of the university, and being part of a team that ensures those systems operate safely, reliably, and efficiently is something I genuinely enjoy.

Want to keep track of the largest startup funding deals in 2026 with our curated list of $100 million-plus venture deals to U.S.-based companies? Check out The Crunchbase Megadeals Board.

This is a weekly feature that runs down the week’s top 10 announced funding rounds in the U.S. Check out last week’s biggest funding deal roundup here.

U.S. startups announced sizable funding rounds at a steady clip during a truncated holiday week, with energy and AI leading the way.

Houston-based energy startup Joulent secured the biggest round, a $1.75 billion strategic financing, followed by Together AI, a developer of infrastructure for companies running open source AI models, and LeapXpert, a provider of compliance tools for enterprises.

Other big rounds were for companies focused on therapeutics, homebuilding, and even lacrosse.

1. Joulent, $1.75B, energy: Houston-based Joulent, a provider of energy infrastructure focused on the demands of artificial intelligence and other compute-intensive industries, raised $1.75 billion in a strategic investment backed by National Grid through its National Grid Ventures arm.

2. Together AI, $800M, AI infrastructure: Together AI, developer of an infrastructure layer for companies running open source AI models, secured $800 million in Series C financing. Aramco Ventures led the round, which set an $8.3 billion post-money valuation for the San Francisco-based startup.

3. LeapXpert, $180M, compliance: LeapXpert, a provider of tools for tracking enterprise communications for compliance needs, closed on $180 million in growth financing. Riverwood Capital led the financing for the New York-based company.

4. 8090 Solutions, $135M, AI software development: Redwood City, California-based 8090 Solutions, developer of a platform for building enterprise software with coordinated AI agents under human-led oversight, picked up $135 million in a round led by Salesforce

. The company, founded in 2024, counts prominent startup investor Chamath Palihapitiya as co-founder and CEO.

5. Beeline Medicines, $126M, biotech: Boston-based Beeline Medicines, a startup focused on precision therapies for autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, secured $126 million in Series A extension funding backed by Bain Capital, CPP Investments and Bristol-Myers Squibb. The financing follows a previously disclosed $300 million Series A.

6. (tied) Premier Lacrosse League, $100 million, professional sports: The Premier Lacrosse League, a men’s professional lacrosse league in North America, closed a $100 million Series E financing round led by Ares Management and Joe Tsai. New York-based PLL said the deal represents the largest capital raise in the history of professional lacrosse.

6. (tied) Twelve Labs, $100M, video-based AI: Twelve Labs, a San Francisco-based startup developing AI systems trained on video archives, raised $100 million in a Series B round co-led by New Enterprise Associates and Naver Ventures.

8. Higharc, $95M, AI for homebuilding: Higharc, a developer of AI-enabled tools for designing homes and managing workflows around homebuilding, picked up $95 million in Series C funding. Insight Partners led the financing for the Durham, North Carolina-based company.

9. Flare Therapeutics, $85M, biotech: Cambridge, Massachusetts-based Flare Therapeutics, a startup targeting transcription factors to develop treatments for cancer and other ailments, raised $85 million in Series C funding led by Third Rock Ventures and Nextech Invest.

10. Venice, $65M, AI privacy: Venice, developer of a platform enabling private, surveillance-free access to a wide array of AI models, secured $65 million in Series A funding led by Dragonfly. The round set a $1 billion valuation for the 2-year-old Sheridan, Wyoming-based startup.

Methodology

We tracked the largest announced rounds in the Crunchbase database that were raised by U.S.-based companies for the period of June 27-July 2. Although most announced rounds are represented in the database, there could be a small time lag as some rounds are reported late in the week.

title: Battery metals recovery runs into stop-start EV market - Academia - The Jakarta Post
description:
The battery metals bust has run its course.
While changes in supply dynamics have shaped the most recent boom-and-bust cycle in battery metals, demand has not stopped growing.
The drag on battery demand has been partly cushioned by a shift to larger vehicles requiring larger batteries, BMI notes.
It's a reminder that not all battery metals are created equal in what is an ever-evolving arms race for cheaper, more efficient chemistries.
Higher battery metal prices mean higher battery prices, which can themselves act as a drag on demand.
text:
The battery metals bust has run its course. Prices of lithium, cobalt and nickel have all recovered from their 2024-2025 lows.

This has largely been a story of supply restraint.

The world's dominant cobalt producer, the Democratic Republic of Congo, has restricted exports since February last year.

Indonesia, which exerts similar control over the nickel supply chain, has used quotas to rein in its runaway mining sector.

Lithium's recovery has been largely down to the market. Two years of super-low prices took a heavy toll on both incumbent producers and new projects. But Chinese authorities' suspension of the giant Jianxiawo lithium mine has helped.

This is still very much a work in progress, with immediate price evolution beholden to policy makers in Kinshasa, Jakarta and China's Jiangxi province.

But some of the previous gloom has lifted from these markets. The focus now turns to whether demand is strong enough to underpin higher price levels.

While changes in supply dynamics have shaped the most recent boom-and-bust cycle in battery metals, demand has not stopped growing.

Global lithium-ion battery deployment in 2025 was six times that of 2020, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).

The driver has been the electric vehicle (EV) sector, which accounts for 70 percent of total lithium-ion battery deployment.

But after surging 20 percent year-on-year in 2025, EV sales have hit a bumpy patch this year.

Global sales growth was just 0.9 percent in January to May, according to consultancy Benchmark Mineral Intelligence (BMI).

The headline figure masks sharply divergent regional performance, however.

Sales in North America fell by 25 percent year-on-year, reflecting the removal of US tax credits in September.

China, the world's largest EV market, also saw sales contract by 15 percent in the first five months of 2026. The drag on battery demand has been partly cushioned by a shift to larger vehicles requiring larger batteries, BMI notes.

Europe, by contrast, registered 26 percent year-on-year growth and the rest of the world grew even faster at 89 percent, reflecting an acceleration of Chinese EV exports, particularly to the rest of Asia.

Grid-scale battery storage is rapidly emerging as an additional lithium demand driver.

Global installations have grown more than 20-fold in the last five years and the sector accounted for 15 percent of battery demand in 2025, according to the IEA.

The global roll-out of renewable energy systems means rising demand for batteries to improve grid reliability when the sun doesn't shine and the wind doesn't blow.

China is halfway through a three-year plan to more than double new energy storage capacity to 180 gigawatts by 2027. More installations will be required if Beijing is to meet a five-year target of generating half the nation's power from renewable energy by 2030.

Battery storage offers lithium some offset to the rise of sodium-ion batteries in the Chinese automotive market but does little to help either cobalt or nickel.

Grid storage batteries use lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP), which contains neither metal.

It's a reminder that not all battery metals are created equal in what is an ever-evolving arms race for cheaper, more efficient chemistries.

LFP is currently the winner of this race, both for energy storage and automotive batteries, where it has taken a 50 percent market share, according to the IEA.

But some Western automakers are understandably reluctant to commit to what is a Chinese-dominated chemistry.

Cobalt and nickel are, for now, holding their own.

Consultancy Adamas Intelligence provides a granular monthly snapshot of metals deployed in passenger EVs.

While the average amount of lithium used per battery was up by 7 percent year-on-year in April, reflecting the shift towards LFP and bigger batteries, average cobalt and nickel usage were both unchanged from a year earlier.

Higher battery metal prices mean higher battery prices, which can themselves act as a drag on demand.

Lithium carbonate prices may already be testing buyers' ability to absorb a near-threefold cost increase since the middle of last year.

Analysts at consultancy Project Blue estimate that current pricing has reached break-even levels for some grid storage projects. They go on to warn that "the risk of demand destruction grows if prices keep rising."

That's a strong reason to believe that the recent battery metal bust won't once again become a battery metal boom.

But market forces are now intertwined with policymaking, adding an extra layer of unpredictability to metals that have until now been defined by an inability to align supply and demand.

---

The writer is columnist for Reuters. The views expressed are personal.

text:
The Indiana State Department of Agriculture has announced the launch of a new $500,000 cost-share program aimed at helping farmers in southwest Indiana adopt conservation practices that improve soil health and protect local water quality.

The initiative, named the Indiana Management of Agriculture Enhancements (IMAGE) Cost-Share Program, comes at a time when agricultural regions nationwide face increasing pressure to curb nutrient runoff while navigating high operational costs for farmers.

The program will offer financial assistance to producers across 23 counties in the southwest portion of the state, covering up to 75% of eligible project costs with a maximum reimbursement of $10,000 per producer.

Agricultural conservation efforts often face economic bottlenecks, as the upfront capital required to shift management practices or install new infrastructure can be prohibitive for independent operations. State officials emphasized that the new funding is specifically structured to bridge that financial gap.

“Conservation practices are often some of the best investments producers can make, but installation costs can often be a significant hurdle,” said Don Lamb, director of the Indiana State Department of Agriculture. “With this new cost share program, ISDA will be able to financially assist more producers looking to improve their soil health.”

The initiative is funded through a $500,000 allocation from Clean Water Indiana, a state fund overseen by the State Soil Conservation Board. To implement the program, the ISDA is partnering with local Soil and Water Conservation Districts, the federal Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS), and regional conservation specialists.

Eligible conservation practices targeted by the funding include pasture and hay planting, the installation of watering facilities and livestock pipelines, soil amendments backed by certified tests, and heavy use area protection. The program will also cover select Environmental Quality Incentives Program (EQIP) practices that have completed federal technical documentation.

Beyond localized farm management, state administrators are tying the program directly to broader environmental goals. The initiative is designed to bolster the Indiana State Nutrient Reduction Strategy, an ongoing effort to prevent sediment, phosphorus, nitrogen, and other agricultural pollutants from entering the state’s river systems and waterways—a critical concern for the broader Mississippi River basin.

The initial rollout will cover a wide geographic footprint in the southwestern quadrant of the state, including Brown, Clay, Daviess, Dubois, Gibson, Greene, Johnson, Knox, Martin, Monroe, Morgan, Owen, Parke, Perry, Pike, Posey, Putnam, Spencer, Sullivan, Vanderburgh, Vermillion, Vigo, and Warrick counties.

name: Texas American Energy
title: Data centers say they pay their way; Texas will hold them to it
description:
Electricity rates are likely to rise in the coming years as utilities make long-delayed grid updates, but new Texas law and regulations are designed to ensure data centers pay their own costs.
The bill intends to make data centers and other large load users bear the lion’s share of the electric-infrastructure upgrades their scale requires.
(By most reckonings, about 70 percent of large-load user connection requests in Texas come from data centers.)
“Why are people coming to Texas for data centers?” said Tom Seng, a professor specializing in energy markets at Texas Christian University’s Neeley School of Business, in an interview.
“Vast available land, preferential tax treatment, no state income and low electricity prices.” Seng argues electricity markets work just like property markets.
text:
Texas has become a national hub of artificial-intelligence infrastructure, second only to Virginia as a site for the sprawling warehouses full of giant computer chips that allow our phones to outsmart us. The biggest question in the state and national debate over AI’s voracious electricity need is: who will pay for the grid upgrades to meet the increased demand and associated stress?

The conventional wisdom is that residential users will suffer as rates go up and reliability goes down due to a surge in data-center load. Large-loaders, however, are not freeloaders. Electricity rates are likely to rise in the coming years as utilities make long-delayed grid updates, but new Texas law and regulations are designed to ensure data centers pay their own costs. The extent of the rise in costs will depend on two factors: whether generation demand and capacity are matched and how transmission costs are divided.

Forecasts for long-term load demand are still in flux. In its most recent forecast, the Electricity Reliability Council of Texas estimated long-term load growth will rise fourfold from the 2023 peak of 85,500 megawatts to 367,000 in 2032. Texas regulators have asked ERCOT to revise that estimate, however, arguing it’s inflated by the inclusion of speculative large-load projects unlikely to materialize.

Texas Senate Bill 6 is intended to deter highly speculative projects and to prevent residential customers from carrying more than their fair share of infrastructure costs. The bill intends to make data centers and other large load users bear the lion’s share of the electric-infrastructure upgrades their scale requires. (By most reckonings, about 70 percent of large-load user connection requests in Texas come from data centers.)

Analysts are divided on whether the bill can achieve its goal of managing the additional demand without a sharp increase in electricity prices.

“Why are people coming to Texas for data centers?” said Tom Seng, a professor specializing in energy markets at Texas Christian University’s Neeley School of Business, in an interview. “Vast available land, preferential tax treatment, no state income and low electricity prices.” Seng argues electricity markets work just like property markets. When house-hunters from California and the Rust Belt moved to Texas for the cheap housing, home prices soon rose. Why would electricity be any different?
