Model 3 and Model Y accounted for 467,762 of the quarter's deliveries, or roughly 97% of total volume. Other models — including the Model S, Model X, Cybertruck, and Semi — contributed 12,364 units [1]. Tesla's energy storage division deployed 13.5 gigawatt-hours, up more than 50% from Q1 [2].

Production totaled 451,758 vehicles, meaning Tesla delivered roughly 28,000 more cars than it built during the quarter. The company had carried approximately 50,363 unsold units from Q1, and the drawdown suggests it cleared a substantial portion of that backlog [1].

The delivery figure crushed every major sell-side estimate. Bloomberg consensus stood at 396,466 vehicles; Tesla's own investor-relations consensus tracker showed a median of 408,609; Goldman Sachs had penciled in 420,000; and Barclays sat at 418,000 [1].

The sell-off reflects a market that has moved past volume as the primary variable for valuing Tesla. At roughly 204 times forward earnings on a 4% net-margin automotive business, the stock's valuation leaves little room for ambiguity on profitability [1].

Investors are focused on whether Tesla maintained healthy per-unit economics while pushing deliveries to a record. The company has cut prices repeatedly since late 2022, and the question of whether cost reductions have kept pace with those cuts will not be answered until the July 22 earnings report [2].

A potential headwind looms in the United States, where Cox Automotive has projected a 20% decline in domestic Tesla sales for Q2, driven partly by the expiration of federal EV tax credits [2]. Consumer backlash against CEO Elon Musk's political activities — which contributed to sharp European sales drops in early 2026 — also remains a factor, though some regional recovery is underway [5].

Tesla's China wholesale deliveries reached 254,551 vehicles in Q2, a 33% year-over-year increase, with June alone contributing 89,091 China-made Model 3 and Model Y units — Tesla's strongest single month of 2026 [2]. European demand also showed signs of stabilizing: French registrations more than doubled in June, Sweden rose 56%, and Denmark climbed 39% [2].

Despite the recovery, Tesla continues to trail BYD in the global battery-electric vehicle race. The Chinese manufacturer delivered 557,090 fully electric vehicles in Q2, maintaining a lead of roughly 77,000 units and reclaiming the global BEV sales crown after briefly ceding it to Tesla in Q1 [3].

Full-year analyst consensus for Tesla stands at approximately 1.65 million vehicles, which would represent barely 1% growth from the 1.64 million units delivered in 2025 [1]. Tesla would need to sustain near-record quarterly volumes in the second half to meaningfully exceed that target.

All eyes now turn to Tesla's Q2 earnings report on July 22, when the company will disclose revenue, gross margins, and average selling prices — the metrics that will determine whether the delivery surge translated into profitable growth or was driven by aggressive discounting and inventory clearance [2].

Tesla's $25 billion AI spending commitment, announced during Q1, adds another dimension to the earnings call. Shareholders want clarity on how the company plans to balance capital allocation between its core automotive business and its expanding AI, robotics, and autonomous-driving ambitions [5].

The stock is down 12.7% year-to-date and 10.3% over the past six months, though it remains up 24.4% over the trailing twelve months [4]. Tesla trades at $392.82, well below its 52-week high of $498.83 [4].

text:
In less than a decade, the decarbonization efforts enshrined in the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) of 2022 will bring annual investments into domestic renewable energy deployment from $64 billion last year to nearly $114 billion in less than a decade, according to a new Wood Mackenzie report.

This will be the case by 2031, according to “Boom time: what the Inflation Reduction Act (Act) means for U.S. renewables manufacturers.” Wood Mackenzie, an energy research and consultancy group under Verisk, set out to assess how the IRA legislation could impact the country and the renewables industry and ultimately found that impact would mean something more like changing the whole field.

“The IRA will completely reshape the renewables supply chain in the U.S., incentivising the reopening of shuttered facilities as well as provide opportunities to build entire equipment supply chains from scratch,” Daniel Liu, principal analyst at Wood Mackenzie and lead author of the report, said.

The IRA, one of the Biden administration’s key legislative focuses early on, will influence the scale of growth in different ways, such as through major expansion of U.S. renewables equipment manufacturing capacity. Some of the largest spikes to come will be in solar utility installed capacity. However, the capacities of solar distributed, both offshore and onshore wind and storage deployments, will continue to tick upward as well.

Still, Liu highlighted wind as being the largest beneficiary in the future. Currently, the United States has enough manufacturing capacity to supply most domestic demand for turbines until 2031, although it must endure a near-term shortage of U.S.-produced equipment. Utility solar P.V. will have a harder time meeting domestic demand and manufacturing capabilities, in his view, due to a small solar manufacturing base and major forecasted growth in the sector, complicated further by U.S. manufacturing costs that are between 16-33 percent higher than imported equipment.

“It’s high stakes for U.S. equipment sales, as the IRA provides incentives that cut the manufacturing cost of solar panels, storage equipment, and wind towers in the U.S. by anywhere from 4 percent to 30 percent,” Liu said. “This, along with tariffs on some imports, potentially puts domestic manufacturing on a cost-competitive footing with imported equipment.”

Some of the likeliest game changers in the IRA are from advanced manufacturing production credits – a tax credit for U.S.-made renewable equipment – and tax credit-based incentives for developers of U.S. renewable projects that purchase domestically produced equipment. The latter has specific thresholds, though: 40 percent of all equipment in a project installed before 2025 must be domestically manufactured, with a 20 percent requirement for offshore wind being the exception, while after 2026, the overall equipment requirement will rise to 55 percent and the offshore wind requirement will rise to match after 2027.

title: Philly-area heat wave could push electricity demand to record levels - WHYY
description:
Air conditioners are running on full blast as a dangerous heat wave bakes the Philadelphia region.
All that electricity use could push demand on the regional grid to record levels Thursday afternoon.
But the regional grid operator, PJM Interconnection, predicts it’ll have enough electricity to meet demand over the next few days, if electric power plants and the lines that carry electricity over long distances perform as expected.
The grid operator has asked power plants and transmission line owners to defer routine maintenance so that they are all available for use.
PJM may also ask big electricity users that have agreed in advance to lower their usage during emergencies to do so.
text:
This story is part of the WHYY News Climate Desk, bringing you news and solutions for our changing region.

From the Poconos to the Jersey Shore to the mouth of the Delaware Bay, what do you want to know about climate change? What would you like us to cover? Get in touch.

Air conditioners are running on full blast as a dangerous heat wave bakes the Philadelphia region. All that electricity use could push demand on the regional grid to record levels Thursday afternoon.

But the regional grid operator, PJM Interconnection, predicts it’ll have enough electricity to meet demand over the next few days, if electric power plants and the lines that carry electricity over long distances perform as expected.

“The system’s tight,” said Jeff Shields, a spokesperson for PJM. “But we think we should be fine.”

High temperatures can affect the grid in multiple ways. They can increase outages of gas and coal-fired power plants if equipment overheats, and more electricity running through transmission lines can cause lines to heat up, sag and break, said Suzanne Glatz, an energy consultant and former infrastructure planner at PJM.

But PJM is taking steps to increase the grid’s capacity and decrease demand.

The grid operator has asked power plants and transmission line owners to defer routine maintenance so that they are all available for use. PJM may also ask big electricity users that have agreed in advance to lower their usage during emergencies to do so.

Avoiding blackouts amid dangerously high heat

The U.S. Department of Energy has also given PJM permission to direct local utilities to require data centers and other big electricity users to switch over to their own backup electricity generation if needed to avoid blackouts for residential and other customers. Shields said PJM will only use this tool as a last resort.

“[PJM is] leveraging every one of the tools that they have available to them, which gives me confidence that we won’t have any issues this week,” Glatz said.

These measures do not require action from residential customers, PJM said. Glatz recommended residential customers still try to conserve energy by avoiding running multiple electric appliances during the hottest part of the day and closing their blinds.

Glatz said she does not expect the heat wave to cause blackouts in the PJM region, which serves 65 million people across Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, and part or all of Maryland, Virginia, Washington, D.C., West Virginia, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio and Tennessee.

While random disruptions such as a thunderstorm knocking down a power line could present additional challenges, the grid is designed with contingencies in place to absorb a certain number of generator and transmission outages, she said.

“We have all these factors built in already to protect against unexpected issues,” she said. “There’s enough margin.”

Late last year, an auction PJM uses to secure commitments from power plants so that electricity supply meets future demand failed to reach the grid operator’s goal for a buffer of excess supply, raising the risk of power outages starting next summer.

text:
Harrisburg, PA – The Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) has proposed two permit updates that will prevent Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) “forever” chemicals in biosolids from polluting farm fields and groundwater. The updated permits introduce monitoring requirements for the first time for wastewater treatment facilities that produce biosolids for land application.

“Pennsylvania continues to lead the way in protecting residents from PFAS chemicals. Three years ago, we published the first standalone drinking water safeguards in Pennsylvania history, years ahead of the federal government, and today we are taking steps to keep forever chemicals out of our food and out of our groundwater,” said DEP Secretary Jessica Shirley. “These updated permits will give the farmers of Pennsylvania peace of mind that the biosolids they use to fertilize their fields are not going to come with PFAS contamination.”

“Farmers need reassurance that what they spread on their fields is safe,” said Pennsylvania Agriculture Secretary Russell Redding. “This is central to public trust and to growing safe, healthy food that also protects our water resources for the future. In crafting thoughtful, intentional public policy we must consider established scientific data, coupled with public and industry perspectives to ensure our success in protecting soil, water, and food systems.”

Under the updated permits, wastewater treatment facilities would have to monitor PFOS and PFOA in any biosolids they produce for land application. PFOS and PFOA are two forever chemicals that have been linked to health issues like cancer.

The permits would also require that wastewater treatment facilities with PFOS or PFOA in biosolids over a certain threshold develop a plan to reduce the amounts of the chemicals in the wastewater. The updated permits would also allow wastewater treatment facilities to accept food waste in their digesters.

DEP developed the revisions to these permits through a robust two-phase stakeholder engagement process. First, beginning in January 2025, DEP convened a 16-member Data Gathering Team to review available data and practices in other states regarding PFAS in biosolids. With the results from the Data Gathering Team in hand, DEP then formed a Biosolids Working Group to discuss proposed updates to the general permits. This group included the Pennsylvania Municipal Authorities Association (PMAA), Pennsylvania Water Environment Association (PWEA), Mid-Atlantic Biosolids Association (MABA), the Pennsylvania Septage Management Association (PSMA), Delaware Riverkeeper Network, Chesapeake Bay Foundation, PennAg Industries, PA Farm Bureau, Pennsylvania Department of Agriculture (PDA), and DEP.

The draft permits are published in the Pennsylvania Bulletin(opens in a new tab). DEP will hold a 60-day comment period that will open July 4, 2026 and close at 11:59 PM on September 2, 2026. All comments will be taken into consideration. Comments may be submitted through DEP’s eComment platform(opens in a new tab) or by emailing ecomment@pa.gov (emailed comments must include the originator’s name and address). The permits are PAG-07 (General Permit for Beneficial Use of Exceptional Quality Biosolids) and PAG-08 (General Permit for Beneficial Use of Biosolids). An additional permit for septage biosolids (PAG-09) is also available for public comment.

In January 2023 DEP finalized regulations limiting PFOS and PFOA in drinking water, the first time that Pennsylvania has ever set a drinking water standard independent of the federal government, which was still years away from implementing drinking water limits. DEP continues to investigate sources of PFAS contamination throughout Pennsylvania.

For more information, visit the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection’s Website(opens in a new tab)

text:
The Trump administration is apparently departing from a landmark Biden-era report that detailed human health risks including cancer from farms contaminated with “forever chemicals.”

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) this week issued a draft guidance document criticizing a draft Biden administration risk assessment detailing health hazards from applying contaminated sludge to farmland.

The Biden-era assessment detailed the risks posed by forever chemicals that are spread across farmland in a type of fertilizer known as “sewage sludge.”

If finalized, it could have laid the groundwork for eventual restrictions on the practice of applying contaminated sludge to farmland.

However, the Trump document, from EPA water chief Jessica Kramer, said that the Biden-era assessment “exhibited a number of serious flaws that have caused confusion.”

Kramer wrote that the agency failed to conduct a national survey of the chemicals in question.

She also said that the Biden administration “only evaluated sewage sludge management practices with higher potential for human health risk” saying this does “not reflect the majority” of actual uses.

Kramer, in her document, offered “voluntary recommendations for potential ways to mitigate risks” posed by the chemicals.

Critics of the Trump move say that the administration is walking away from regulating and its duty to protect the public from “forever chemicals” which are also known as PFAS.

“This guidance document completely fails to address the risk to human health and the environment from PFAS-contaminated sludge and the reality is that sewage sludge has been spread on millions of acres of farmland nationwide, harming people across the country by exposing them to PFAS in soil, water, crops, meat, fish, dust, et cetera,” said Erica Kyzmir-McKeon, director of communities and toxics at the Conservation Law Foundation.

“With this guidance document, they have made clear that they have no intention of regulating PFAS and sludge, and that they are going to continue to allow PFAS contaminated sludge to be spread on farmland throughout the country,” she added.

However, Kramer, in a written statement, said that her guidance document “will provide Americans with commonsense recommendations that can protect public health, while also supporting wastewater systems and beneficial use of biosolids [sewage sludge] when appropriate.”

PFAS are the name of a family of chemicals that are known for their waterproof and stain resistant properties. They’re a family of thousands of chemicals, but the documents in question pertain to two of the most well-studied and highly toxic PFAS, called PFOA and PFOS.

Some farms have become contaminated with forever chemicals through the land application of sewage sludge containing PFAs — a byproduct that comes from treating wastewater produced by households and businesses.

This sludge has been applied to some farms as fertilizer, and when it contained PFAS, it led to those chemicals being spread as well.

The Biden-era document, issued during the final days of the administration, said that under certain conditions, applying contaminated sludge to land could cause unacceptable risks of cancer and other health effects.

In particular, it detailed potential risks from drinking milk and eating beef or eggs from contaminated farms. It also found possible risk from drinking water sourced from contaminated groundwater or eating fish from a lake affected by farm runoff.

Kyzmir-McKeon said that states are taking actions like banning the use of sewage sludge and or limiting the levels of PFAS that can be in sludge — which could be replicated at the federal level.

Kramer’s document also outlined steps that states have taken, including bans, but she noted that they are “presented to illustrate options that some states have considered and implemented, and they should not be interpreted as the EPA’s endorsement of these actions.”

Kramer, in the new document, recommended that farmers avoid using sewage sludge near sources of drinking water or fishing and avoiding applying sludge to land that may have high risks for human exposure. She said that wastewater treatment plants should consider monitoring for PFAS in sewage sludge and adding liners to areas where it disposes of the sludge.

Kramer also noted that about 20 percent of sludge is sold directly to the general public or applied to areas that regular people are exposed to. She said that the general public should research suppliers and not use sludge when cultivating high risk foods like leafy greens and root vegetables — and where egg laying hens have access.

text:
The Solar Energy Industries Association's (SEIA’s) Finance, Tax and Buyers Seminar, which returned to New York June 23-24, once again brought together developers, investors, lenders, tax credit buyers, corporate energy purchasers, attorneys, insurers, manufacturers and policy professionals for one of the renewable energy industry's premier finance conferences.

At a time of unprecedented change in federal energy policy, trade dynamics and project financing structures, the seminar served as an invaluable opportunity to connect with clients, partners and new industry colleagues while hearing directly from experts and practitioners navigating these challenges in real time.

The conference's overarching message was one of cautious optimism. While the solar industry continues to face the near-term end of the investment and production tax credits, a steadily increasing stack of tariffs, uncertainty on foreign entity of concern (FEOC) rules, permitting, and interconnection, market participants are not standing still, as noted in other Notes from Novogradac blogs. They are seeking solutions and adapting by developing new diligence frameworks and continuing to evaluate financing and underwriting options and capital deployment for projects needed to meet America's rapidly growing electricity demand.

A Market in Transition

The conference agenda reflected an industry undergoing significant transformation.

Sessions covered everything from federal policy developments and market outlooks to project financing, tax equity, transferability, storage and corporate procurement strategies. A recurring theme throughout the conference was that clean energy finance is becoming increasingly sophisticated as the industry moves from an incentive-driven market to one where compliance, documentation and risk management increasingly determine project success.

One particularly timely session, "The New Tax Equity Market–How Hybrid Models are Altering the Status Quo," explored how tax equity structures continue to evolve in response to transferability and changing market dynamics. Panelists discussed the increasing use of hybrid financing structures that combine traditional tax equity with tax credit transfers, debt and other capital sources to optimize project economics and broaden the investor base.

Speakers said that transferability has fundamentally changed the financing landscape, creating greater flexibility for sponsors while also introducing new diligence considerations and opportunities for innovative financing structures. Rather than replacing traditional tax equity entirely, the market appears to be evolving toward a broader toolkit of financing solutions tailored to different project types and sponsor needs.

Other sessions focused on storage financing, debt markets, insurance products and the role of corporate buyers in supporting clean energy deployment. Across each discussion, messages remained consistent: demand is surging, renewables are the fastest and still most affordable solution, and the market continues to innovate despite policy and regulatory headwinds and increased uncertainty.

FEOC Takes Center Stage: Building a Compliant Supply Chain

The central theme of industry discussions and one of the conference's most anticipated topics was implementation of the FEOC rules and what they mean for project finance and clean energy supply chains.

During his keynote remarks, Deputy Assistant Secretary for Energy, Strategic Initiatives and Tax Administration at the U.S. Department of the Treasury (Treasury), Don Snyder, emphasized that Congress intentionally designed the FEOC provisions to incentivize the development of a clean energy industry that is not controlled by prohibited foreign entities. He said that many lawmakers, particularly in the Senate, were increasingly reluctant to continue providing federal incentives to supply chains and market participants that they believed had benefited from unfair competitive advantages abroad.

At the same time, Snyder stressed that Congress also recognized the need to provide the industry with sufficient statutory direction and safe harbors to continue investing and building projects while Treasury develops additional guidance and regulations. He reiterated that Treasury values stakeholder engagement and is actively working through complex issues involving ownership, debt, effective control, documentation requirements and anti-circumvention provisions.

Those themes carried directly into the panel discussion, "FEOC & Domestic Content: Navigating the Mandatory Floor and the Tax Credit Adders," led by Novogradac Partner Tony Grappone, who also leads the Novogradac-hosted Renewable Energy Working Group.

During the panel, Grappone succinctly captured the market's view of the new rules: Domestic content is an adder. FEOC is existential.

This important distinction resonated throughout the discussion. Missing a domestic content bonus will affect project economics, but failing FEOC compliance can eliminate credit eligibility entirely.

Panelists said that the industry remains in a transitional period as legal, insurance and financing markets develop frameworks to assess and price FEOC risk. The average pricing differences between legacy Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 48 investments and new IRC Section 48E investments indicating the more demanding compliance requirements of Section 48E and the significant additional diligence costs and transaction complexity.

Several practical themes emerged:

FEOC supply chain diligence should be a top priority and not delayed.

Material assistance and supplier certifications are becoming central transaction issues.

Outstanding effective control rules are of primary concern, and analyses will require extensive diligence on counterparties and ownership structures.

Insurance products remain limited, with many policies currently serving as narrow placeholders that exclude areas potentially affected by future guidance.

Perhaps most importantly, panelists emphasized that the market is already adapting. Developers, investors, insurers and advisors are increasingly working toward standardized diligence processes, certifications and documentation packages that can support transactions in this new environment.

The message from both Treasury and market participants was clear: FEOC compliance is not a temporary hurdle to overcome. It is becoming a permanent feature of clean energy project finance and a key determinant of which projects and supply chains will remain competitive in the years ahead.

Transferability Continues to Mature

I (Josh Morris) also led the impactful QuickTalk: “Key Things to Watch Out for in Transfer Deals" on the seller-side perspective on how the transfer market is evolving and what sponsors should do to position transactions for success.

The central message was that sellers are not simply selling tax credits, they are selling confidence. As the transfer market matures, buyers increasingly expect sponsors to present clear, organized and well-documented evidentiary files.

Beginning-of-construction (BOC) documentation received particular attention. Sellers should treat their BOC position as an evidence package, not simply a tax memorandum. Particularly in light of the Sections 48E and 45Y July 4 deadline for solar and wind, sponsors should have clear support for the BOC test being relied upon, the date construction began, the work performed or costs incurred, and the documents supporting that position.

Buyers are also increasingly focused on continuity. They want to understand not only whether construction began but what happened afterward and whether the project continued to move forward.

It’s important to be wary of aggressive strategies that appear to create eligibility on paper without meaningful project activity, including:

Generic equipment purchases not tied to a specific project,

Artificially small scopes of work,

Generic, non-custom inventory allocations that cannot be tied to a specific facility, and

After-the-fact memoranda that are stronger than the underlying facts.

Even technically arguable positions can create pricing pressure, delay closings, or cause buyers to walk away if they fail a commercial diligence "smell test."

The discussion also focused extensively on FEOC and material assistance cost ratio (MACR) diligence.

The new guidance is workable because taxpayers can now build a process around it–but not workable in the sense that sellers can ignore supply chain diligence until closing and solve everything with a generic certificate.

The challenge is often practical rather than technical. Procurement files were created to purchase equipment and build projects, not necessarily to support tax credit diligence. Sellers increasingly need supplier information, certifications, component-level data, cost information and defensible methodologies for applying the MACR rules.

Timing is also critical. Supplier responses can be incomplete, delayed or raise additional questions. As a result, sellers should begin FEOC diligence early rather than waiting until a tax credit buyer is already in the data room.

The cleanest investments are not necessarily those with no issues. They are the investments where sellers understand the breadth issues that could come up, document the facts, explain the risks and provide buyers with a clear and reconciled diligence package.

Interconnection: The Biggest Challenge in Project Finance

Another standout discussion was "From Queue to Capital: Navigating Interconnection Risk for Large-scale Solar & Storage Projects."

The panel explored how delays and uncertainty in the interconnection process are increasingly affecting project finance and deployment.

One of the key takeaways is that developers and capital markets struggle most with adapting to and financing unexpected increases in costs and project delays. Extended delays, uncertainty, steadily mounting costs and last-minute, unexpected cost increases are often the undoing of initially viable, non-speculative projects, particularly mid-sized to smaller distributed projects that are less able to absorb increases in costs, according to an article by PV Magazine.

Projects can have millions to tens of millions of dollars or more tied up in interconnection deposits for years while final upgrade costs and energization timelines remain uncertain. Those delays create substantial carrying costs, extend construction financing and effectively freeze capital that could otherwise be deployed into additional projects.

Panelists also discussed the growing financial exposure associated with Federal Energy Regulatory Commission Order 2023's readiness requirements and withdrawal penalties, which can expose projects to millions of dollars in financial commitments if they exit the queue late in the process, according to a Zonevex blog.

They highlighted the recent changes approved for the Southwest Power Pool's Consolidated Planning Process, which integrates transmission planning and interconnection into a single framework intended to provide greater cost certainty and faster timelines. The process introduces standardized interconnection charges and pre-identified interconnection locations that may ultimately serve as a model for other regions, according to SPP.

Meanwhile, another important development highlighted is the novel use of surety bonds. FERC permitted the use of bonds and other forms of financial security in addition to traditional letters of credit and cash deposits in FERC Order 2023-A. This additional flexibility may help reduce the capital burden associated with queue participation.

The panel also explored flexible interconnection, grid-enhancing technologies (GETs) and advanced transmission technologies (ATTs). While these innovations have tremendous potential to unlock additional capacity and accelerate deployment, they also create new risks and introduce new questions around reliability, cost allocation and revenue predictability.

The consensus was clear: these tools are important complements to transmission expansion but are not substitutes for it.

The Market Must Forge Ahead

The industry faces no shortage of challenges.

FEOC compliance requirements continue to evolve. Trade disputes and tariffs are reshaping supply chains. Permitting and interconnection delays remain significant obstacles. Additional guidance is still needed on ownership, debt, material assistance and effective control determinations.

Yet despite these uncertainties, the market is moving forward.

Developers continue signing procurement contracts and building inventories. Manufacturers continue investing in domestic and non-Chinese international supply chains. Investors and tax credit buyers are developing new diligence frameworks and documentation standards. Insurance markets are beginning to build products that can support transactions as additional regulatory clarity emerges.

Perhaps most importantly, the industry increasingly recognizes that it does not have a supply shortage problem, it has a FEOC-compliant supply problem.

Global manufacturing capacity remains abundant, domestic manufacturing continues to expand rapidly, and developers are increasingly organizing procurement and financing decisions around FEOC compliance rather than simply lowest-cost sourcing.

The challenge is not whether projects can be built, it is determining which supply chains will remain commercially viable and eligible for federal tax incentives.

The discussions throughout SEIA's Finance, Tax & Buyers Seminar suggested that the renewable energy market is entering a new phase. Success will increasingly depend not only on technology and financing innovation, but also on the ability to navigate complex compliance obligations, manage geopolitical and supply chain risks, and provide investors with the certainty necessary to continue deploying capital.

The market should not wait for perfect guidance. It needs to continue building the tools, processes and partnerships necessary to move forward and begin establishing well diligenced and documented FEOC compliance based on the statutory rules and guidance available. And if SEIA’s seminar was any indication, the industry is on its way toward creating the compliance and financing infrastructure needed to support the next generation of clean energy investment.
